content:
【LLM評価の盲点】自社モデルを優遇？「LLM-as-a-Judge」のバイアスと信頼性を高める対策

LLMが他のLLMの出力を評価する「LLM-as-a-Judge」という手法、開発の現場でよく使われていますよね。しかし、ここには非常に興味深い「バイアス」が隠されていることが明らかになりました！

55種類のモデルに互いの出力をブラインド評価させた実験（Multivac Evaluation）によると、QwenやAnthropicなどのモデルは自社ファミリーのモデルに対してスコアを甘くつける「同族愛（Nepotism）バイアス」が統計的に確認されたのです。一方で、MistralやMetaなどのモデルは、なぜか自社モデルを過剰に厳しく評価する「自己懲罰」という真逆のユニークな挙動を見せました。モデルごとの個性が評価にまで影響しているのはとても面白いですね！

特に注意が必要なのが「コード生成」の評価です。バグがあって動かないコードを、LLMジャッジがなぜか好んで高く評価してしまうといった不整合が起きており、単一のAIによる評価はかなり不安定であることが分かりました。正しいコードかどうかの客観的な判断（Ground Truth）を無視してしまうリスクがあるため、LLMの主観だけに頼るのは危険ですね。

この課題を乗り越え、評価の信頼性を高めるためのアプローチとして、以下のような設計が提案されています！

・コードや数学などの明確なタスクでは、AIの主観ではなく「自動テスト（Verifier）」を最優先にする
・異なる開発元のモデルを組み合わせた「異質なジャッジパネル」を構築し、相互に監視させる
・「甘口」「辛口」といったジャッジの偏りを、ブラッドレー・テリーモデルなどの統計的手法で補正する

これからのAIシステム構築やモデル選定では、ベンチマークの数値をそのまま信じるのではなく、こうした評価自体のバイアスを考慮した多角的な設計が必須になりそうです！

この原因になる「KVキャッシュ」という会話の記憶データをギュッと圧縮（量子化）してメモリを節約する技術があるのですが、普通は圧縮するとAIの頭が急に悪くなってしまうのが大きな悩みでした。

ところが、新しく登場した「Gemma 4 QAT 31B」はこの圧縮に対してもの凄く強い耐性を持っていることが分かりました！✨

その秘密は「QAT（量子化を意識した学習）」という独自の仕組みにあります。
あらかじめ「後で圧縮されること」を見越して、モデルの内部数値を小さくコントロールしながら賢く学習させているんです。だから、4ビットや8ビットといった極端な圧縮をかけても、情報がほとんど失われません！

KLD（圧縮前後のズレを示す指標）のスコアを見ても、驚くほど劣化が抑えられています。

これによって得られるメリットがこちら👇
・【圧倒的なコスト削減】少ないVRAMで動かせるので、高価なGPUを何枚も用意しなくてOK！
・【大量の同時処理】1台のサーバーで、同時にたくさんのユーザーのリクエストを捌けるようになります！
・【サクサク長文処理】メモリを気にする必要がなくなるので、長いドキュメントの読み込みも快適そのもの！

最近、AIが自律的に動く「エージェント」の開発がすごく盛り上がっていますが、またまた面白いプロジェクトを見つけちゃいました！✨

それが、HTMLメールを自動で作成・管理できるツール「mailcue（メールキュー）」です！

このツールの素晴らしいポイントは、最近話題の「MCP（Model Context Protocol）」という共通規格を内蔵している点！

しかも、送るメールはただの文字だけではありません。崩れがちなHTML/CSSや、スマホ対応を簡単にする「MJML」というテンプレート言語をAIに直接理解させて、ブランドイメージを壊さない「最高に見栄えの良い」メールを自動で組み上げてくれます！🎨✨

さらに嬉しいのが、「Gemma 4」や「Qwen 3.6」といったオープンなAIモデルを、自分のパソコンなどの「ローカル環境」で動かすことを前提にしているところ。

また、長文を読み込ませる際の精度を保つために、モデルを軽量化する「クァンティゼーション（量化）」や、一時的な記憶領域である「KVキャッシュ」の管理も欠かせません。Qwen 27Bなどの巨大モデルを動かすときは、モデル自体の重みはQ5〜Q6に抑えて、KVキャッシュをQ4で独立管理するといった賢い運用が非常に効果的です！

システムメモリ（メインRAM）へのスワップ（退避）による速度低下を防ぐチェックポイント管理など、工夫次第で予算を抑えつつプロ級の推論環境が構築できます。夢の超高速ローカルAI環境をぜひ手に入れましょう！🚀

【Sana 1.6Bを8.6倍軽量化！極限の3値化技術「Ternary Quantization」が凄すぎる✨】

画像生成AI「Sana 1.6B」を、驚異の「8.6倍」も軽量化したモデルが公開されて話題になっています！

なんと元のファイルサイズ「3.21GB」から、わずか「374MB」にまで極限までスリム化されているんです。

この劇的な圧縮を可能にしたのが「Ternary Quantization（3値化）」という高度な技術。AIの重み（パラメータ）のデータを、シンプルに「-1、0、1」の3つの値だけで表現することで、メモリ使用量を劇的に減らしています。

「でも、そこまで削ったら画質がボロボロになるんじゃ…🤔」と心配になりますよね。

そこがこの技術の賢いところで、「グループ・ワイズ・スケール」という仕組みを採用しているんです！すべてのデータを一律に削るのではなく、画像生成に重要な役割を持つ「条件付け層」など（全体の約5%）は、あえて高品質な精度のまま残してあります。このメリハリのおかげで、圧倒的な軽さと高い生成品質を両立させているんですね。

これなら、VRAM（ビデオメモリ）が少ない古いGPUや普通のPCでも高品質な画像生成をスムーズに楽しめます！将来的にはRaspberry Piのような省電力デバイスやモバイル環境での動作も期待できそうで、コストを抑えてAIを活用したいクリエイターや企業にとっても大きな一歩になりそうです。

こうした極限圧縮の技術がどんどん進化していけば、AIがもっと身近な存在になりそうで本当にワクワクしますね！

title: In 1988, Tom Selleck stepped away from "Magnum, P.I." (1980) after years of fame, long workweeks, and national attention. His daughter Hannah was born that December, and his life quietly changed direc
content:
In 1988, Tom Selleck stepped away from "Magnum, P.I." (1980) after years of fame, long workweeks, and national attention. His daughter Hannah was born that December, and his life quietly changed direction.

He did not disappear because success had failed him. He stepped back because success had taken too much space, and he wanted room for marriage, fatherhood, privacy, and ordinary mornings.

By then, Selleck was not just another handsome TV star. He was one of the most recognizable men in America, with the mustache, the relaxed charm, and the Hawaiian-shirt image people instantly connected with him. But behind that easy screen confidence, he had already learned how loud fame could become. Cameras followed. Stories grew. Privacy became something a person had to fight for, not something he simply had.

His love story with Jillie Mack began far away from Hollywood, in London, while he was filming "Lassiter" (1984). Jillie was performing as Rumpleteazer in "Cats", and Selleck kept returning to watch the show. Jane Seymour later remembered how strange it seemed that he kept talking about the musical and going back again and again. The real pull was not the stage lights. It was Jillie. Her agent later said, "They had dinner one night and it went on from there."

That small dinner became a life decision. When Jillie’s contract ended, she moved to the United States, and Selleck treated the relationship like something precious, not something to feed to the tabloids. He had already been married before to Jacqueline Ray, and he had adopted her son Kevin. He understood that love could be damaged by pressure, schedules, and public noise.

On August 7, 1987, Tom and Jillie married near Lake Tahoe, Nevada, in a secret chapel ceremony. Only a few family members were there. His brother Bob helped arrange it under fake names, Tom Jenkins and Suzie Mark, so the press would not find them. Even the minister was expecting two ordinary people, not one of television’s biggest stars.

The wedding almost had another problem. Years later, Selleck remembered the commotion when they realized they had forgotten the marriage license. He said, "That’s what I remember most about the wedding. And Reverend David saying I’ll sign the thing anyway." The reverend helped fix the problem, and Selleck looked back at the whole day as an adventure he would never trade.

Then came Hannah Margaret Selleck on December 16, 1988. Instead of treating fatherhood like something squeezed between scripts, Selleck changed the entire shape of his life. He and Jillie moved to a secluded Ventura County ranch, a 65-acre property that had once been a working avocado farm. It had belonged to Dean Martin before changing hands, and Selleck bought it in 1988.

The ranch was not a celebrity decoration. It became work. It became fences, trees, horses, dust, repairs, and quiet discipline. Selleck tended the avocado trees himself until drought hurt the crop. The land gave his family distance from Hollywood and gave Hannah a childhood with space, animals, and responsibility. Jillie later said they both believed it was the best environment for Hannah to grow up in.

Selleck explained the choice in the simplest way. "I’m a fairly private person. And I’ve always treasured the balance between work and time with my family. It’s always about them." That sentence says almost everything. He was not rejecting acting. He was refusing to let acting become the whole house.

He also said, "My relationships and my ranch keep me sane. I do grunt work and I make the rounds. I like watching things grow. It’s a retreat." For a man whose fame was built on images, the ranch gave him something real. A tree did not care about ratings. A fence did not care about applause. A marriage could not survive on charm alone. It needed attention, routine, and protection.

That is why the Tom and Jillie story feels different. It is not loud. It is not scandalous. It is not built around dramatic breakups or comeback headlines.

content:
Never Miss an exam Attempt : How I Finally Became a #CA After 8 attempts....

I cleared CA Foundation, CA Intermediate, and Group 2 of CA Final in my first attempt. I was staying in a hostel in Pune and my articleship training was smooth. 

Life felt on track.

Then reality hit in November 1999. For the first time in my life, I failed an exam — Group 1 of CA Final. It was devastating. 

Back then, there were almost no coaching classes for Audit and Corporate Law. We had to rely completely on self-study from ICAI material or few books avaialble that time.

I appeared again in May 2000. This time, I cleared all subjects but missed the aggregate by just 4 marks. That pain still stays with me. (Unfortunately, I lost the marksheet of that attempt and could not attach in collage). 

The failures continued in November 2000 as well. By then, the stamp of failure had started affecting me. People began questioning my abilities.  To handle this, I started taking up part-time accounting assignments while continuing to work in the same CA firm where I completed my articleship.

The attempts in May 2001, November 2001, and May 2002 were extremely stressful. ICAI had changed the paper pattern of MAFA, and many questions were coming from outside the study material or even coachin class studies,  something many students have updated facing in recent attempts. But that was not an excuse for me because at Final level, you require EXPERT KNOWEDGE as per ICAI guidelines mentioned in study material.

In December 2001, I shifted back to Aurangabad (now Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar). I joined a CA firm as a full-time Audit Assistant. The job involved extensive travelling. 

At 23 years of age, I had to support my family financially . 

Despite everything, I never missed a single attempt.

In November 2002, I again missed the aggregate — this time by 7 marks. This was my 7th attempt for Group 1.  By then, I was handling significant office responsibilities, including internal audits, which were both time-consuming and thankless. I used to study whenever I could find time.

Then came the May 2003 attempt. I could manage only 15 days of study leave because of an important assignment with a strict deadline. 

The Advanced Accounting paper was very tough and lengthy — I could attempt only 65–70 marks. I genuinely thought it was over this time. However, I had prepared MAFA from Ravi Kishore Sir’s book, especially the capital market chapters. I was able to attempt the entire paper, which gave me confidence. I then performed well in Audit and Corporate Law too.

After 8 attempts, I finally cleared Group 1 of CA Final. I scored the highest marks in MAFA at the Aurangabad centre. I was also lucky to get 40 marks in Advanced Accounting. Had I failed in Advanced Accounting, I would have got group exemption in the other three papers. But this time, my persistence paid off.

To all students who are facing repeated failures:
Failure is neither new nor rare in CA exams. I was part of that majority for almost four years. 

During this period, I faced immense mental pressure, self-doubt, and external judgment. But my aim never allowed me to accept defeat. I never skipped any attempt — and that single decision played a big role in my success.

Since 2003, I have had the privilege of mentoring over 30 article assistants and students, many of whom have cleared CA and are doing well in their careers. 

If you are currently struggling with failures, remember this: Don’t lose courage. Your consistent efforts matter more than you think. 

Strengthen your mind, stay focused on your goal, and never miss an attempt.

Success eventually comes to those who keep showing up and it changes your perspective.

Eva Marie Saint is 101, still alive, and now one of the last bright human links to the Hollywood that gave the world Marlon Brando, Cary Grant, Alfred Hitchcock, black and white television, studio glamour, and old fashioned movie grace. 

Born on July 4, 1924, in Newark, New Jersey, she has lived long enough to become more than a screen legend. She has become a living bridge.

But the most touching part of Eva’s story was never only the Oscar.

It was the family she built.

In 1951, Eva married director, writer, and producer Jeffrey Hayden.

The marriage lasted 65 years.

Not six years.

Not sixteen.

Sixty-five.

Until Jeffrey passed away in 2016 at the age of 90.

Hollywood has always celebrated dramatic romances, public breakups, and headline-making relationships. Eva and Jeffrey chose something quieter.

Something lasting.

Together, they raised two children, Darrell and Laurette. Over time, the family grew into grandchildren, great-grandchildren, and four generations connected by the same woman at the center.

That is why her 100th birthday felt so emotional.

It was not simply a famous actress reaching a remarkable age.

It was a mother, grandmother, and great-grandmother looking around a room filled with people whose lives existed because hers had come first.

Speaking about the milestone, Eva said, “I’m looking forward to spending my 100th birthday in Los Angeles with my dear, dear family. Four generations of family members will be gathering together.”

That single quote says everything.

She witnessed Hollywood transform from live television to streaming platforms.

From black-and-white dramas to digital blockbusters.

But the greatest transformation happened at home.

She watched generations grow up.

Her own career began with a breakthrough most actors only dream about.

In *On the Waterfront* (1954), she played Edie Doyle opposite Marlon Brando. The performance earned her the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress in her very first major film role.

The moment was already extraordinary.

Then life added another chapter.

Eva was nine months pregnant when she accepted the Oscar.

Two days later, her son was born.

Career history and family history arrived almost at the same moment.

Five years later came *North by Northwest*.

Working with Cary Grant and Alfred Hitchcock, Eva became Eve Kendall, elegant, mysterious, intelligent, and unforgettable.

The role introduced audiences to a different side of her talent.

Years later, she recalled Hitchcock’s unusual approach.

“He didn’t talk about acting. He worked with me from the outside in. My hair, my makeup, my shoes, my jewelry, my purse, my gloves.”

With Brando, she showed warmth and emotional courage.

With Grant, she showed style and intrigue.

Very few actresses mastered both worlds so completely.

Her success continued through television as well.

She won a Primetime Emmy for *People Like Us* in 1990 and remained active across film, television, theater, and voice work.

Yet fame never seemed to become the center of her identity.

Family did.

And at the heart of that family was Jeffrey Hayden.

He stood beside the young actress, the Oscar winner, the Hitchcock star, the mother, and eventually the grandmother and great-grandmother.

When he died, he left behind not just a marriage, but an entire lifetime shared together.

Today, Eva Marie Saint remains the oldest living Oscar winner and one of the last surviving stars of Hollywood’s Golden Age.

But perhaps her greatest achievement is something no award can measure.

She carried fame without letting it define her.

Hollywood remembers the performances.

Her family remembers the woman.

And at 101, Eva Marie Saint still shines with the same quiet grace that first made audiences fall in love with her decades ago.

Have you ever stood in a funeral room where flowers tried to make loss look gentle? 

The air feels different..people speak softly. Children stay close to their parents. Someone stares at the floor because they cannot bear to look at the casket again.

Rooms like that tell the truth about this life.

Jesus speaks to His frightened disciples as a Savior who knows every hallway sorrow will make us walk.

“In my Father’s house are many rooms... I go to prepare a place for you... I will come again and will take you to myself, that where I am you may be also” (John 14:2–3).

Heaven is more than a vague wish floating somewhere beyond the stars. Jesus called it His Father’s house. He spoke of rooms, preparation, return and presence. The promise reaches higher than going somewhere better. The promise is that He comes for us and brings us to Himself.

Death tries to make the silence feel permanent. Jesus speaks into the ache and says He has already gone ahead. He will come again.

The last room a Christian fears will never have the final word.

Christ does.

And for everyone who belongs to Him, the door opens home.

content:
A whole generation can be changed by one opportunity.

Years ago, the University of Zimbabwe could not offer her a place in Medicine. She was offered Chemical Engineering instead.

But she had only one dream: to become a doctor.

Then an unexpected opportunity came from a university in Russia.

The timing was terrible.

There was no financial plan for it. I had to scramble resources and postpone some very important bills to make it happen.

Then COVID struck.

She spent her entire first year studying online, unable to travel.

When she finally got clearance to go to campus, war broke out.

Every year brought a new reason to worry.

Yet she stayed focused.

We stayed hopeful.

And today, she has graduated as a medical doctor.

We now have a whole Dr in the family.

The most educated person in our family history.

As her uncle, I couldn’t be prouder.

This moment is bigger than one graduation.

It is a reminder of what the diaspora is really doing across Africa.

Behind many success stories back home is a brother, sister, uncle, aunt, parent or cousin abroad quietly paying fees, sending money, sacrificing comfort, working double shifts, missing family events, and carrying responsibilities nobody sees.

People often measure diaspora success by the cars we drive or the countries we live in.

I measure it differently.

I measure it by the lives we help transform.

When I left Zimbabwe, I had one small bag, no job, and only US$150 standing between me and poverty.

I had dreams, but no guarantees.

I never imagined that one day God would use my journey to help raise a doctor.

This is why I will always say: diaspora is not just migration.

It is investment.

It is sacrifice.

It is generational empowerment.

To every person in the diaspora supporting a child, sibling, niece, nephew, or student back home:

Keep going.

You may think you are just paying school fees.

One day you may realise you were helping build a doctor, engineer, teacher, entrepreneur, scientist, or leader.

And that investment will outlive all of us.

Today, our family celebrates a doctor.

Tomorrow, she will change lives.

When a Plane Hit Beijing’s Monument to State Power

A small aircraft bit into Beijing’s tallest building. Online, many quickly dubbed it “Beijing 9/11.”

https://t.co/PI99S3EKzM

Instead of discussing the incident, I want to tell a deeper story about the building itself.

China Zun — 中国尊 — is not just a skyscraper. It is political architecture.

“Zun” refers to an ancient Chinese ritual vessel, but the word also carries the meaning of reverence, hierarchy, and power. Fittingly, this building is a monument to all three.

As I described in my book, after the 2008 financial crisis, Beijing began to rethink its attitude toward the Western market model. The Party concluded that the West had exposed its weakness, while China’s state system had demonstrated its strength. State-owned enterprises could be ordered to invest immediately. They did not need to wait for the market, monetary transmission, private-sector confidence, or shareholder approval. They could simply execute political will.

That marked the start of a decisive shift toward 国进民退 — the advance of the state and the retreat of private enterprise.

The origin story of Beijing’s new CBD, and of China Zun itself, captures this perfectly.

Liu Qi had been Beijing’s mayor and later Party Secretary from 1999. Around 2008 or 2009, according to a story circulated among Beijing elites, he had an encounter with Bo Xilai, then Party Secretary of Chongqing and a rising second-generation red aristocrat.

Bo reportedly mocked him to his face: what had Liu built in Beijing after so many years? Shanghai had Pudong and its skyscrapers. Shenzhen had its skyline. What had Liu done to show in Beijing?

Soon after, Beijing pushed forward a massive new CBD expansion next to the existing Guomao business district.

The irony is rich. Foreign observers often assume Chinese projects come from grand, rational, long-term planning. Sometimes they do. But some also come from bureaucratic ego, political competition, and personal humiliation.

By then, the rules of the game had changed.

The private sector might have had capital, experience, and ambition, but it no longer had the political standing to lead such a project. All plots in the new CBD were reserved for large SOEs.

Naturally, CITIC was chosen to build the tallest tower.

CITIC was one of China’s most powerful SOE conglomerates, with businesses spanning finance, banking, mining, trading, real estate, and much else. It had long been led by prominent princelings. At the time, its chairman was Kong Dan. His father, Kong Yuan, had been a senior figure in the early Communist intelligence system. His mother had served as secretary to Zhou Enlai, Mao’s long-time premier and right-hand man. His brother, Kong Dong, later became president of Air China.

This is how power worked in China.

I had dinner with both brothers around that period. My airport business had many dealings with Air China, and my company was developing a site next to CITIC’s then headquarters — the site that is today the Bulgari Hotel Beijing.

We were interested in participating in the new Beijing CBD. But once we understood the political direction, we decided against it. Private companies had no meaningful role. The future belonged to SOEs.

That is why China Zun matters beyond architecture.

It is not merely Beijing’s tallest building. It is a monument to a particular era: the post-2008 confidence of the Chinese state, the reassertion of SOEs, the narrowing space for private capital, and the belief that political command should replace market dynamism.

So when a small aircraft hits China Zun, the incident is alarming in itself.

But the building it struck carries its own history.

It is a symbol of the China that emerged after 2008: taller, more state-led, more politically controlled, and more convinced of its own model.

The question now is whether that model, once projected upward in steel and glass, is beginning to show cracks of its own.

8 non-sexual lessons every mother should teach her daughter. ✨
1. Self-respect comes before love.
If she doesn't value herself, others won't either. Teach her that no relationship is worth sacrificing her dignity for.

2. Believe actions, not words.
Anyone can make promises. Character is revealed through consistency, effort, and behavior over time.

3. Not everything deserves your reaction.
Some battles aren't worth your energy. Peace often comes from knowing what to ignore.

4. Privacy is power.
Not every goal, struggle, or success needs an audience. Moving quietly protects your peace.

5. How you speak to yourself matters.
The relationship she has with herself will shape every other relationship in her life.

6. Rejection is redirection.
Sometimes what doesn't work out is protecting her from something she cannot yet see.

7. Discipline matters more than motivation.
Motivation fades. The habits she builds when she doesn't feel like showing up will define her future.

8. Know your worth.
Teach her to never beg for love, attention, or respect. The right people won't require her to. ✨

Can't tell you how much I wish movies like these were still being made.

And these are just a few of my favorites. There's also White Fang, Little Giants, The Sandlot, Blank Check, Richie Rich... the list goes on.

They were filled with real people, real locations, real extras, real friendships, and real stakes (at least when you were 10 years old). 

The heroes weren't perfect. Kids failed. They got hurt. They were scared. There was a little light cursing, an awkward romance, and a lot of heart.

I think about when Henry realizes his Mom was actually the star pitcher, or when Junior Bevel sees his Dad wearing a Jamaican Bobsled Team shirt, or the first "Ducks Fly Together" chant.  

Today's family movies can still tell great stories, but I miss this era of real life adventures. There was something about watching real kids in a real world that made you believe you could have an adventure too.

Maybe it's nostalgia, or maybe we really did lose something worth keeping.

content:
Intvw with Lee Ainslie of Maverick, Graham & Doddsville, 2014 -- five excerpts on L/S equity, talent, and "No Holds" portfolio construction

1. Tiger Mindset - 'you should be the smartest person alive on your sector.'

"At Tiger you were essentially expected to be the foremost authority on a small number of stocks. For the investments you oversaw, no other public investor should know more about those companies than you did."

2. Talent evaluation: 

"The most important components we gauge include competitiveness, mental flexibility and emotional consistency—that last trait is surprisingly important. 

This is a very stressful business. We are all human, and we all make mistakes. How one responds to those mistakes and whether someone can keep a level head and make thoughtful decisions is critical. 

Conversely, how does one respond to a few big wins? With some folks, early success leads to inflated confidence that may slow the recognition of a mistake."

3. On 'No-Holds' Portfolio Management in L/S: 

"I think I have read almost everything that Warren Buffett has written, and I agree with more than 95% of his thinking, but this is one area where I disagree. 

I understand the tax impact of turnover, but nevertheless, I would argue that an investor should be able to overcome the negative tax consequences of shorter-term holdings through more efficient use of capital. 

For example, if I am starting a new fund, and my portfolio is a blank sheet of paper then I will evaluate the potential return of every potential investment from the prices the market is offering that day. I can decide how much risk I am willing to take to achieve expected returns, and I can evaluate how each opportunity compares to every other opportunity to develop a portfolio which I believe represents the optimal use of capital. 

In my view, tomorrow, I should go through the exact same process taking into account any new information including changes in the price of securities. If I conclude that a different portfolio would be preferable then I should buy or sell securities to get to the portfolio that I believe represents the optimal use of capital once again."

4. No-Holds (continued): 

"The “no holds” concept simply reflects the approach that every investment should represent a very compelling risk/reward opportunity from current prices, and if that’s not the case then that capital should be redeployed into positions that are viewed as very compelling at current prices. 

In the perfect world, every member of our investment team is pounding the table to increase the size their positions every day until they are at a maximum size in terms liquidity or risk contribution. 

When somebody tells me that they don’t think we should sell a stock, but that they wouldn't buy more at the current price either, then that investment probably does not represent one of our very best uses of capital—unless the size of the position is already at a maximum from a risk perspective. 

We want our portfolio invested in the most attractive use of capital today at current price points, and if a certain position no longer represents that then we should sell. 

Sometimes, people have a hard time with this because this philosophy often means we are reducing or exiting a position before it’s reached our expected price. For example, if a stock is 10% away from our original target price, we are likely to sell because we think there are many other opportunities with greater upside. 

Conceptually, our team has to accept this concept of “no holds.”

5. On Valuation

"To be clear, I think that valuation is a critical component of understanding where investment opportunities may lie. But I think many “value investors” purely focus on that metric and may ignore other important considerations. 

It’s one thing if you have a very cheap stock and reasons to believe that the cheap valuation will not persist: there's a new management team, there's an activist shareholder, they’re restructuring, they just made a decision to buy back stock, and so forth. I believe it is important to identify a catalyst that should benefit the valuation. 

The approach of simply identifying a very cheap stock that often has been cheap for a while and then just crossing your fingers and hoping the world will wake up and be willing to assign a higher valuation one day soon is not a very effective approach in my judgment. 

So while we place great emphasis on valuation in our investment decisions, valuation alone should never be the driver of either a long or a short investment."

END: Advice to students interested in an investing career

"Two things: first, read a lot. Read as many investment books as you can get your hands on. I've been able to learn something from almost every book I have ever read.

Secondly, the path to an investment career is not necessarily to work at a hedge fund or at a large mutual fund complex. You can start your career by simply improving your understanding of how different industries or companies work or how Wall Street works. Any brokerage firm or Wall Street firm can be a path to an investment career. A lot of people move from the sell-side to the buy-side over time. We probably have as many former McKinsey consultants as we do former Morgan Stanley investment bankers."

The most brutal thing to understand about life is that you don't get what you want, you get what you believe you deserve.

You can do everything right. You can get the opportunity, the money, the relationship, the dream handed to you on a plate. But if underneath it all you still don't believe you deserve good things, your mind treats the good life as a mistake that needs correcting. To your brain, a gap between reality and what you feel you deserve isn't success, it's an error, and your subconscious works to close that gap by pulling reality back down to match.

This is why people self-sabotage right when things start going well. The good relationship shows up and they pick fights or push the person away. The money comes in and somehow leaks back out within a year. It doesn't look like sabotage in the moment, it feels like bad luck or things just not working out. But it's too consistent to be bad luck. It's the feeling of not deserving it, dragging them back to what they think they're worth.

And this happens even when life completely changes on its own. Lottery winners go broke. People lose the weight and gain it back. People escape a toxic relationship and end up with someone just like the one they left. Everything around them changed, but the feeling of what they were worth stayed the same, so they ended up right back where it started.

This is the second part of my post about my father on his birthday and the life lessons from him.

I was reminded of this thanks to a discussion a couple of days ago on one of my WhatsApp group on acknowledging and celebrating our wins.

Most of us when we achieve a goal, just move on to the next one. 

We hardly ever look back to see how far we have come...or the fact that we probably already are way ahead of where we dreamt of being once upon a time

In my first year of my career when doing my first IPO as an investment banker, I remember taking a flight from Bombay to Kolkata in the morning doing a press conference and broker conference there and taking the evening flight to Hyderabad. I was completely thrilled that I was in three different cities in a single day and of course staying in fancy hotels... now we groan at the thought of flights 

My father would always say with a great deal of pride: 

- When I came to Lucknow after Partition (he had just finished his 12th) nobody wanted me to study but  I was determined and anyway after 1 year  I topped & got a scholarship l, so nobody had to spend on my studies after that 

- I topped MSc and I got a job immediately in the university 

- I built the house (the one I grew up in) with high quality materials and facing the directions I wanted after only 8 years of working which was unheard of at the time 

And so on 

For the next 50 years he was proud of all this besides the fact that his students revered him as an outstanding teacher (my students' love and respect is my real wealth he used to say)

He also took pride in the fact that he could help anyone who asked him for help - that his hand would always be in the giving position (you can say in a  sense he manifested that)

He was not a rich man by general standards but in his head he was a rich man 

Because of that there was always a feeling of abundance at home

I remember him saying, "Maine to  acche karm kiye the, Maine to acchi zindagi bitai" 😄

We can always try for more but let us not forget to celebrate how far we have come

And it was not as if everything in his career went smoothly. 

He was after all a complete outsider in deeply casteist Uttar Pradesh.

For example, his promotion was delayed (in an academic life, there are only two promotions - so it is a Big deal) but he did not let it get him down - I know of so many people who had heart attacks or even died due to stress about the promotions.

For him the important part was that he was teaching which was the love of his life and yet his job gave him enough free time to play bridge, meet people, have long holidays and do whatever else he desired in life.

He thought that nothing could be better and hence wanted all of us to follow in his footsteps - although none of us did 😊

So much of life is not what happens to you but how you react to it.

Important lessons to learn 🙏

content:
Diane Keaton died on October 11, 2025, at 79, leaving behind grief and two children who knew her simply as Mom.

To millions, she was the unforgettable star of *Annie Hall* (1977), *The Godfather* (1972), and *Something’s Gotta Give* (2003). At home, she was Dexter and Duke Keaton’s mother.

That was the love story Diane built quietly.

No wedding ring.

No grand public romance.

No turning her children into celebrities.

She had famous relationships throughout her life, but marriage never became the center of her world.

Motherhood did.

Diane was 50 when she adopted her daughter, Dexter, in 1996. Dexter had been born on December 15, 1995. Five years later, she adopted her son, Duke, who was born on February 8, 2000.

For Diane, success no longer sounded like applause.

It sounded like children filling a home with life.

She once explained her choice with characteristic honesty.

“Motherhood was not an urge I couldn’t resist, it was more like a thought I’d been thinking for a very long time.”

That sentence felt completely like Diane.

No fairy tale.

No dramatic revelation.

Just a quiet truth.

She had carried the thought for years until one day it became her life.

Motherhood changed everything. The worries that had once focused on her career and herself shifted toward her children. She became protective, attentive, and deeply devoted while still trying to give Dexter and Duke room to grow.

In 2007, she revealed how she wanted their lives to be.

“They have no interest in what I do, which I think is very healthy. We live a relatively normal, well, sort of normal life.”

That small pause said a lot.

Diane understood that nothing about her life was entirely ordinary, but she worked hard to give her children as much normality as possible.

Dexter and Duke grew up mostly outside Hollywood’s spotlight. Dexter married Jordan White in 2021, and Diane stood proudly beside her as a mother rather than a movie icon. Duke remained even more private, appearing only occasionally with his family.

One of their rare public moments together came in August 2022 when Diane placed her hands and feet in cement at TCL Chinese Theatre.

Both children stood beside her.

Proud.

Present.

Asked what it meant to have them there, Diane answered with one word.

“Everything.”

Then she added, “I love them.”

After her passing, those words carried even greater meaning.

The awards were not everything.

Dexter and Duke were.

On the first Mother’s Day without her, Dexter shared a tribute filled with longing, writing that she missed her mother’s voice, hugs, presence, and everything that made her feel at home.

For what would have been Diane’s 80th birthday, both children honored her in their own way. Dexter tattooed “la di da” on her wrist. Duke chose “weird old world.”

Small tributes.

Family language.

Lasting love.

Diane never became a wife, and she never felt the need to apologize for it. Her life was not defined by the family she married into.

It was defined by the family she chose.

She gave the world unforgettable characters, but Dexter and Duke received the role no audience ever owned.

Her quietest love story was the one she lived at home.

Some of us will live forever.

And if you’re reading this, that may or may not be you.

I am so bullish on this that I just renamed my company to Immortals.

Below:
+ why I think this
+ early signs of success
+ how to increase your odds

Yes, I know this sounds crazy.

Immortality has been an ambition for humanity since the beginning of recorded history.

The immortality I’m referring to is specific: increases in life expectancy will outpace the rate of aging. Meaning, we will no longer, by default, expect to die of natural causes.

I believe this for three reasons.

#1: Immortality already exists

Biology can reverse some features of aging, and in a handful of organisms escape it almost entirely. For example, a sperm and an egg from two people in their 30s carry the legacy of bodies that have aged for decades (the egg in particular has been arrested inside the mother since before she herself was born), yet they combine to produce an embryo that resets the aging clock to zero.

The immortal jellyfish goes further and resets itself within one lifetime, reverting its adult cells to an earlier stage through transdifferentiation and starting its life cycle again. And in the lab, scientists have begun doing this deliberately, making induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) from mature adult cells such as skin fibroblasts, and using partial cellular reprogramming to turn the clock back in the tissues of living animals.

#2: AI offers new potentials

Biology is a hard problem. For most of history that complexity was beyond native human capacity. AI was made for this complexity. The clearest demonstration so far is protein folding. Predicting the three-dimensional shape a protein folds was an unsolved problem for roughly fifty years, and it mattered because a protein's shape determines what it does in the body.

DeepMind's AlphaFold2 effectively solved it in 2020, reaching a median accuracy of 92.4 out of 100, a level long thought to require the slow, painstaking work of crystallizing a protein and solving its structure by X-ray crystallography. It then released predicted structures for over 200 million proteins, nearly the entire catalogued protein universe, in a fraction of the time anyone expected.

#3: Early signs are encouraging 

These aspirations are not imaginative. With the current tools in biotech Sid Sijbrandij, the co-founder of GitLab, was diagnosed with an aggressive bone cancer, osteosarcoma in his vertebrae. He treated his own disease like an engineering problem, he used AI to help direct several experimental, personalized therapies in parallel and drove the cancer into remission after standard medicine had given up. Around the same time, an Australian named Paul Conyngham, with no medical or biology background, did something similar for his dog. He used AI to help design a personalized mRNA vaccine targeting the specific mutations in his dog's tumor, and after it was given alongside another immunotherapy and within a few months the main tumor had shrunk by roughly three-quarters.

How to increase your odds…

I. Don’t die in the meantime

We don’t know when these longevity therapies will become available. Your goal is to be around when they come out. Buy yourself as much time as possible by looking after your body to the best of our scientific knowledge. Good diet, sleep, exercise will get you 80% of the results.

II. Find your achilles

Longevity therapies will likely be outcome specific.  Individual specific drugs/therapies that target specific things like…

> prevent and remove arterial plaque
> prevent and reverse neurodegeneration
> specifically target and eliminate cancers, or pre cancerous legions
> prevent frailty and muscle loss, and regain muscle mass, strength and, bone density
> reverse skin aging
> rejuvenate eye health 
> restore lost hearing
> etc

We don’t know what therapies will be available first. Your goal is to find what your body is struggling with most and keep that problem at-bay until a therapy is available that can fully cure or reverse it. 

For example, do you struggle with cholesterol? Blood glucose control? Cognitive decline? Find your achilles heel and reduce your risk systematically.

III. Invest in the future

There are three macro trends happening on planet earth right now, and the people who bet on these areas have the highest risk + reward.

> AI
> Immortality
> Energy

As we know, power comes in many forms: money, social, political, health, etc. Those that can collect power in these fields will have the greatest chance of positioning themselves in the Immortal future.

With time, Immortal therapies will become broadly available.

Good morning homies...

Let's get back to a basic truth most don't think about. Even though they know intuitively it is the single biggest factor of success in every area of life...your words. More specifically the words you speak to yourself. 

Do you know your speech, the words you both speak aloud (especially so) and inside your mind are rewiring your brain? The words you speak to yourself are either building you up or breaking you down. They are making you stronger or weaker by the moment. 

Think about it. How do you feel when someone sings your praises? Or tells you how much they love you? Or how proud they are of you? Or how they appreciate you? Or speaks words of encouragement to you because they see your efforts? It feels quite good right? It boosts your confidence. It wells up inside you a sense of peace. A feeling of strength. A desire to keep moving forward. A feeling of being unstoppable. 

And how do you feel when you are berated by another? When you're told your not good enough. Your efforts mean nothing. Or when someone tells you they hate you or can't stand to be in your presence. That your life will not amount to anything good because you're nothing but a failure. Do you feel on top of the world? Do you feel unstoppable? Or do you feel like giving up and quitting? Not even trying or getting started...

Do you think it is any different when you speak to yourself? In fact, it's worse. You may feel that someone's negativity towards you may be false but it's a seed planted in your mind. And when you don't counteract it with your own words based on belief and fact, they will become the words inside your own mind and eventually manifest themselves out of your own mouth and ultimately in your own life.

In many cases, that person is projecting. But that is for another time. Just know, although they are the object of consternation, they need prayer, mercy and grace from you. But that doesn't mean you need to take it. Quite the contrary. You are not a door mat.

Where you're at in life right now has been a series of choices you made up to this point. But have you ever stopped to ask yourself why you chose the way you did? Have you ever considered those choices were directly related to the words you speak? Because they are. You've been planting seeds, sowing to what builds you up or breaks you down, and harvesting from the fields that you yourself have cultivated. 

It's time for the negativity to stop. It's time to take back control of your life. It's time to begin a new journey and step onto the path that will produce a good harvest in your life. It all starts in your mind. For we are told in Romans 12:2, "Do not conform to the pattern of this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind. Then you will be able to test and approve what God’s will is—his good, pleasing and perfect will." And Proverbs 18:21 tells us, "Death and life are in the power of the tongue, and those who love it will eat its fruits." 

Did you catch that? Those who love it will eat its fruits. Fruit can be good and it can be bad. Which one are you going to eat? Will you sow to the spirit of truth and reap a bountiful harvest of goodness in your life? Or will you sow to spirit of lies and reap the bountiful harvest of negativity that produces death and decay.

new phone, new car, new jewellery, etc.

his salary STOPPED.

I wish, above all, to be devout.

Already in my life, I left the world once. In a perverse inversion of monasticism, my life as a vagabond drifter involved the total abandonment of money, security, status, and comfort. I have proven to myself that I can withstand deprivation.

I have also proven to myself what grave sin and evil I am capable of. There is not a sin on the list that I have not touched. In coming home to the Church, I came bearing deep wounds from a radically dark and sinful life.

Therefore, my reversion came as a rescue -- but it came with an asterisk. Because I have already shown myself to be capable of abandoning the world, and of suffering frequent hunger, exposure, persecution, and violence, I know that I have no excuse. Because I owe Christ my life -- for I was on the road to an early grave before I found Him again -- my debt to Him is total. There is not one iota of what I am that is not owed to Him.

There is no reason that I should not forego all other forms of success and ambition in favor of a devout life. I should attend the daily Mass, I must give an hour to contemplation each day, I must tirelessly engage in some form of work that increases the glory of Christ's Church on earth.

I wish to give all the hours of all my days to packing the pews. I yearn to walk the streets, calling the lost home to the shepherd. If there is a way that all of the hours of my days could be spent in conversation with those outside the Church, feeding them, healing them, guiding them home to the Eucharistic Jesus, I would do it.

My prayer is that I can go deeper. That I can become more consistent. That I can dwell in the perfect joy of Jesus Christ for all the hours of my days, radiating some tiny fragment of His love outward onto all that I meet, working tirelessly for Him.

I have no excuse but to go all out. Were it not for Christ and his holy Roman Catholic Church, I would certainly be dead and in hell already. Could I repay Him with laziness and neglect? Could I relax into lukewarmness when my debt to Him came due already the second I made my first general confession? I cannot do that. I must strive to become devout. My life has no other purpose.

I want to be very clear that this is a theory, not an accusation. It’s speculative. But I’ve s
content:
I have a theory about why Ilhan Omar’s net worth skyrocketed and plummeted in her financial disclosures.

I want to be very clear that this is a theory, not an accusation. It’s speculative. But I’ve spent enough time in finance to see this play out.

My theory is about loans.

Omar’s husband, Tim Mynett, was the cofounder of a firm called Rose Lake Capital at the time of her earlier disclosures. Rose Lake Capital has since taken down their website, but they previously marketed themselves as both an investment advisory firm and as a venture capital firm (whether Rose Lake ever actually raised any assets under management is questionable, but we’ll get to that momentarily).

Most people, when they hear that someone works in venture capital, imagine the person to be wealthy. And for top VCs in Silicon Valley, that’s certainly true. But there are now thousands of VC firms, employing tens of thousands of investment professionals. And the industry has an awkward secret:

Most people working in VC don’t have any money.

VCs make the preponderance of their money from carried interest (if you’re not familiar with the term, think of carried interest as a share of the profits a fund generates after it returns capital to the limited partners providing its funding). Many funds never generate high enough returns to produce carried interest for fund managers, and even those that do take eight to 12 years to do so.

Which means that many VCs, unless they’ve had successful exits in the past, don’t have much personal liquidity.

Nobody goes into venture capital to be middle-class, though, and eight to 12 years is a long time to spend not making serious money. So a lot of VCs use a workaround: They borrow money. They either borrow directly against their future carried interest (there’s an entire cottage industry of specialty lenders offering this), or they borrow indirectly against it by including the estimated present value of their future carried interest payments as an asset on their personal financial statements when applying for a mortgage (you can probably see where this is going now).

Let’s say that Omar’s husband expected that Rose Lake would raise $250M and generate a 3x multiple on invested capital (MOIC) over the life of its first fund. Using an industry standard 20% carried interest rate, Rose Lake would collect $100M of carried interest ($250M * 2x * 20%). As cofounder of the company, Tim Mynett would likely be entitled to 20-40% of the carried interest, or $20-40M.

Adjusted for the time value of money, that $20-40M in eight to 12 years would be worth $5-20M, depending on the assumed AUM, the assumed MOIC of the fund, and the discount rate used to calculate the present value. Which aligns almost perfectly with the $6-30M of net worth that Ilhan Omar disclosed in 2024, after reporting de minimis assets every year prior thereto.

So why would Ilhan Omar, a far-left member of “the Squad,” report this much wealth, knowing that it would be a lightning rod for criticism? After all, future carried interest payments are not an asset that requires disclosure; for all intents and purposes, they are hypothetical future income, which she and her husband would have been well within their rights not to disclose at all.

This is where the loan I mentioned above comes in. My theory is that Tim Mynett, at some point prior to Omar’s 2024 financial disclosure, took out a loan based on his future carried interest payments from Rose Lake. The loan may have been directly secured by the carried interest payments, though that strikes me as unlikely (industry lenders generally don’t like to advance funds to first-time VCs who don’t have a successful track record). More likely is that he either took out an unsecured loan or some type of mortgage, the financial disclosure for which listed the present value of his Rose Lake carried interest as an asset (I would expect to see something along the lines of “fair market value of management interest in Rose Lake Capital” in the documents).

Once Mynett included the carried interest as an asset on his personal financial statements, Omar almost wouldn’t have a choice but to include it in her congressional financial disclosure. If she didn’t and if Mynett one day failed to repay the loan, Mynett’s creditors could make a case for bank fraud, commercial lending fraud, or any number of other white-collar crimes.

Why, after all this, though, would Omar report close to zero assets the year after this disclosure? It’s simple: Rose Lake fell apart. Its website is shuttered, no one can find any information about it, and it likely never raised a dollar of assets. Mynett’s stake in the firm—as well as the present value of any future carried interest he would expect to receive—was worth zero.

This is likely the “accounting error” that Omar keeps referencing. It’s not that her accountants added up her checking accounts and 401k incorrectly; it’s that her husband did some back-of-the-napkin math on hypothetically future income to qualify for a loan, and they very quickly realized that said income would never stand a chance of materializing.

Again, I want to emphasize that this is speculation on my part. I am not privy to the facts and circumstances of this situation, and I need to be abundantly clear that I am accusing neither Omar nor her husband of wrongdoing. If facts emerge in the future that contradict my theory, I will be more than happy to issue a retraction of this.

But I’ve spent a long time working in M&A, and I’ve seen all manner of shenanigans when it comes to the personal finances of people in this industry. Unless Ilhan Omar has the world’s most inept Quality Learning Center CPA, this is the ONLY explanation I can think of that would lead to Omar’s reported net worth taking a round trip from essentially zero to $30M back down to zero.

content:
There was a man.. brilliant, successful, respected by everyone who knew him... who was secretly enslaved to something he couldn't shake for over a decade. ⤵️

His name was Augustine.

One of the greatest saints in Church history spent years trapped by lust.

He was intelligent, successful, and respected. Yet he could not find peace. As a young man, he pursued pleasure, relationships, status, and success. He wanted happiness, but nothing satisfied him.

His mother, St. Monica, prayed for his conversion for years.

He kept running from God.

Augustine later admitted how divided he felt. He wanted to change, but he also wanted to keep his sins. In his Confessions, he famously prayed:

→ “Grant me chastity and continence, but not yet.”

Many people know exactly what that feels like.

They know what is right. They know what is sinful. They want God, but they do not want to let go of the things pulling them away from Him.

Augustine searched for answers in philosophy, ambition, and human wisdom. He followed Manichaeism for years, hoping it would explain truth and happiness.

It did not.

While living in Milan, he began listening to St. Ambrose preach. The faith he had rejected started to make sense.

Then came the moment that changed his life.

Overwhelmed by his inner struggle, Augustine heard a voice saying, “Take and read.” He opened the Scriptures and read Romans 13:13–14:

→ “Not in reveling and drunkenness, not in debauchery and licentiousness, not in quarreling and jealousy. But put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the desires of the flesh.”

He later wrote:

→ “No further would I read; nor did I need to, for instantly, as the sentence ended, a light of relief from all anxiety flooded into my heart, and all the shadows of doubt vanished.”

Everything changed.

Augustine was baptized by St. Ambrose at Easter in A.D. 387. He later became bishop of Hippo and one of the greatest teachers in the history of the Church.

The man who could not break free became a saint.

The man who chased pleasure taught the world about grace.

The man who ran from God spent the rest of his life leading others to Him.

His most famous words still confront us today:

→ “You have made us for yourself, O Lord, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.”

Many people are not rejecting God.

They are simply hoping something else will satisfy them first.

💬 What is the hardest thing for people to surrender to God today?

title: Norway wins the most medals at the Winter Olympics, with a population of just 5.6 million. People say it’s because Norway is a winter wonderland, but they’re also elite at triathlon, beach volleyball,
content:
Norway wins the most medals at the Winter Olympics, with a population of just 5.6 million. People say it’s because Norway is a winter wonderland, but they’re also elite at triathlon, beach volleyball, cycling, and as the world is now seeing, soccer.

A big part of their success is how they treat youth sports—and it’s the opposite of what we do in the US and Canada. Here’s what we can learn from Norway:

1. Scorekeeping:

In the US: Youth sports tend to be hyper competitive even at early ages. Leagues almost always keep score.

In Norway: Scorekeeping isn’t even allowed until age 13.

Removing winners and losers keeps the focus on the process not outcomes. It keeps kids engaged longer because it minimizes pressure (and tears) and maximizes fun, learning, and growth. The goal isn’t to win a third grade championship. It’s to love sport and keep playing.

2. Trophies:

In the US: If you give everyone a trophy, you’re creating snowflakes who will never gain a competitive edge.

In Norway: Whenever trophies are awarded, they are handed out to everyone.

If getting a trophy makes young kids feel good, we should give them trophies. Maybe they’ll come back and play again next year!!

As for the creation of snowflakes with no competitive edge—Norway’s athletes are tough as nails and all they do is win.

3. Prioritizing Fun:

In the US: Far too often, the goal is to win.

In Norway: The national philosophy is “joy of sport.”

Youth sports in the US are driven by adults, ego, and money. Youth sports in Norway are driven by fun.

Only half of kids in the US participate in sports. The number one reason they drop out: because they aren’t having fun anymore. In Norway, 93% of kids participate in youth sports. Fun is the foremost goal.

4. Playing Multiple Sports:

In the US: There’s pressure to specialize early and play your best sport year round.

In Norway: Try as many sports as you can before specializing as late as college.

Norway encourages kids to try all types of sport. This reduces injury and burnout and increases all-around athleticism. It also helps promotes match quality, or finding the sport you are best suited for as your body develops, which is impossible if you commit to a single sport too early.

5. Affordability

In the US: There is increasingly a pay-to-play model with high fees for leagues, equipment, and travel. This excludes many kids from playing.

In Norway: It’s a national priority to keep youth sports affordable and therefore accessible for all.

Kids aren’t priced out, which creates opportunities for everyone to participate (and develop into athletes), regardless of their parents’ income level.

Norway’s sporting success isn’t just speculation or a nice story. A large body of research supports their approach:

• Studies show athletes who specialize later in life have a significantly higher chance of becoming elite.
• Soccer players whose motivation is primarily internal (versus external) have more than a 3x better chance of making it to an elite level.
• The number one predictor of whether or not kids stay in sport is are they having fun.
• Parents connect winning to having fun whereas kids say having fun is about being with their friends and learning.

We could learn a lot from Norway:

In the US, 70% of kids drop out of youth sports by age 13. This not only diminishes an elite-athlete pipeline, but it also destroys an opportunity for healthy habits and all the character lessons kids can learn from sport.

In Norway, lifelong participation in sport is the norm. The goal isn’t to have the best 9U team. It’s to develop the best athletes. Those are two very different things. And Norway has the medals to prove it.

CRED charges brands to place offers directly in front of these specific people. 

Second, CRED knows exactly how much money its users earn, how much they spend, and whether they pay on time. 

That is some of the richest financial data available anywhere. They use it to give out personal loans to these same users through partner banks. 

CRED sits in the middle and earns a cut every time a loan goes through. Lending is now more than 50 percent of their revenue.

Third, they have added rent payments, UPI, vehicle management, insurance, travel bookings. 

So, every new feature keeps the user inside CRED for more of their daily financial life. More time in the app means more chances to sell them something.

So to put it simply.

CRED built a club where only creditworthy people get in. Then they sold access to that club to brands and lenders who cannot reach these people any other way.

Basically, I have 1.3 crore rich, financially responsible Indians sitting in my app. Who wants to sell to them?

content:
The LaMelo Ant backcourt should terrify the NBA: a power forward case study.

In full disclosure, I was planning on writing about the importance of playmaking to match the new size this week anyway. I adapted to the recent trade.

Dumping Julius Randle gave the Wolves cap flexibility to make a splash trade to acquire LaMelo Ball from the Hornets. This is exactly what the Timberwolves needed around Anthony Edwards. I described earlier this week how the Wolves need a PG who can shoot and handle the ball. I did not think LaMelo was even an option, and he fits that mold perfectly. For the record, I am generally a skeptic of making splash moves. I prefer roster flexibility and draft picks, but even for me, this is an exception. This fit works even better after the draft this week and the trends from the picks.

This trend looks at the power forward position. Remember your older brother’s power forwards from the 2010s: David West, Paul Millsap, Serge Ibaka, Carlos Boozer. Better versions were Kevin Love and LaMarcus Aldridge. Most of these guys fit the description of big, good rebounder, can be a secondary post defender, can kind of shoot but no threes.

What happened to this archetype? The Golden State Warriors and Draymond Green. The Warriors changed the game with their passing, motion, and shooting, making that big power forward inefficient, old, and slow. Before the Wolves tried to use two bigs, KAT and Rudy, and started the size trend again in a way, power forwards came in all shapes and sizes. From Jayson Tatum, a large small forward who mostly plays on the perimeter, Jaren Jackson Jr., a center’s body who prefers to play as a help defender, a former DPOY who somehow can't rebound. Draymond Green, relatively small but, in my opinion, the second best defender since 2010. Very smart, can switch everything. He can guard on the perimeter and is strong enough to guard smaller bigs.

Don’t look now, but the power forward and big frontcourt are returning. Looking just in the West, I will list a few big projected starting 3-5s:

OKC: J-Dub 6'5, Chet Holmgren 7'1, Isaiah Hartenstein 7'0.

Utah: Lauri Markkanen 7'1, Jaren Jackson Jr. 6'10, Walker Kessler 7'2.

Portland: Deni Avdija 6'8, Toumani Camara 6'7, Donovan Clingan 7'2.

Spurs: Wemby 7'4, plus their bigger guards.

Houston: Amen Thompson 6'7, Kevin Durant 6'11, Jabari Smith Jr. 6'11, Alperen Sengun 6'11.

Dallas: Morez Johnson Jr. 6'9, Cooper Flagg 6'9, Dereck Lively II 7'1.

Grizzlies: Cameron Boozer 6'9 and Zach Edey 7'3.

That is 7 out of the other 14 Western Conference teams projected to start a very tall frontcourt. Size is back in the NBA, likely due to competing with Wemby.

If the trend is to go big, why did the Wolves send their projected starting power forward and all their remaining draft assets to go trade for a point guard? The answer is what Steve Kerr and the Warriors did to make the NBA small a decade ago. The Warriors changed the game with a dynamic backcourt that shot and made more threes than any other backcourt up to that point. But their small lineup that defended and made these bigs run around the court changed the game. Since then, the three ball is something all teams had to incorporate, but they forgot what made these Warriors teams special, and that was their passing.

The last two regular seasons, the Oklahoma City Thunder were the league’s best defense in terms of net rating. They typically started a very tall lead guard in SGA, a big wing defender in Lu Dort, a big do-it-all wing in Jalen Williams, a tall three and post D player in Chet Holmgren, and a center in Isiah Hartenstein. The Thunder went big, and the league followed. Yes, the Thunder have good depth, but their starting lineup is elite. What were the teams that made this Thunder team struggle? It was not the Wolves, the iso heavy, not a lot of passing, slow Timberwolves.
It was the Denver Nuggets and the Indiana Pacers. What do both of these teams have? An elite one of one playmaker and a team that is built around that. Tyrese Haliburton and Nikola Jokic, and their playmaking, are what make these big teams struggle. Their creative motion puts these defenders in bad situations. Jokic has gotten the better of Wemby in their limited matchups, and KAT's playmaking also has made Wemby look human. Meanwhile Indiana ran through the east last season and took the Thunder to 7 with Hali getting hurt in game 7. There is a legit world where they win the finals last year. 

What does this have to do with LaMelo? Last season, the Wolves had a creation issue. Their assist leader was Julius Randle with a measly 4 a game. Ant was doubled a lot and did not have the playmaking to make the defense pay. 

The Wolves were a bottom 6 team in catch and shoot attempts per game but were top 5 in catch and shoot shooting percentage. Meanwhile, the Hornets were 6th in attempts. Most of that was LaMelo’s ability as a ball handler to create space and passing to take advantage. Now add this to the Wolves, who are an elite catch and shoot team. Ant shoots almost 50% on catch and shoot threes. Ayo can make them as well. At this point, the fifth starter is unknown, but the gravity generated by the backcourt can help both Jaden and Rudy unlock their offense. Jaden will get the ball in more opportune times, plus throwing lobs to Rudy. The Wolves already have the pieces for a top-5 offense, and Rudy and Jaden to stabilize a top-10 defense. Opponents will really struggle against going big against the Wolves. The lineup they can run of Ball, Ant, Ayo, Jaden, and Rudy can pass, move, and make these bigs look slow. If Finch can unlock this, the bigs of the West will not have a fun time playing the Wolves.

The three concerns I have seen about LaMelo are maturity, injuries, and defense. To start with maturity, Ball is only 24; he has time to develop this. At the start of his time with the Hornets, the franchise was dysfunctional. His vets were Bismack Biyombo and Gordon Hayward. He had multiple head coaches and finally had a taste of success this season. Compared to Minnesota, Rudy has a well-documented history of taking care of his body, Mike Conley, if he stays, is a great vet, and Ant is one of the hardest workers in the NBA. Plus, a great coach in Chris Finch at keeping a culture. I think the Wolves ecosystem can help him mature into a winning player. 

Injuries have plagued LaMelo at this point of his career. This season, he played the most games, and he also played the least minutes per game. That has to be the recipe: contain his minutes, and he should stay healthier. Along with the Wolves having an elite medical staff, I trust they know this. The Wolves are also exploring bringing back Conley and Bones. They already have Ant and Ayo locked up. Minnesota has the guard depth to limit his minutes and keep him healthy and fresh.

LaMelo's defense has never been great. He does have the size you want in a big guard. This is my biggest concern, but this move is about the playoffs, where intensity brings out the best. If he can’t lock in during the playoffs defensively, he is likely a lost cause, but with the Wolves, I think it can work.

This season is the most excited I think I have ever been for a Timberwolves season in my life. This is a roster that can win at the highest level, and I think it can change the game.

JOKES

I strongly disagree.

Living with my parents has probably been one of the biggest advantages I've had.

I don't pay rent. Because of that, I've had the freedom to make mistakes, try different things, take risks, learn new skills, build projects, and create opportunities for other people.

I've worked with world-class projects, including Webtoons and fintech companies in the US, all from my parents' house.

I've been invited to speak at events in places I've never been before. I've partnered with amazing founders and professionals. I've helped people get their first opportunities. And I did all of that without the pressure of wondering how I'll pay ₦2 million in rent next year.

Some people make a little money and immediately start preaching that everyone should move out. That's terrible advice for many young people.

What happens when the income becomes unstable?

What happens when you don't know where the next client is coming from?

What happens when rent, feeding, transportation, and bills start competing with your dreams?

Many people would never have built anything meaningful if they had those pressures too early.

The truth is, not paying rent gives you something incredibly valuable: time and runway.

Time to learn.
Time to network.
Time to experiment.
Time to fail.
Time to build.

You can literally sit in your parents' house, work with people across the world, attend meetings from your phone, build a business, create jobs, and impact lives. LITERALLY WHAT I AM DOING. 

Some of you will move out and still be introverted. You'll still stay indoors. You'll still have the same habits. Changing location doesn't automatically change your life.

If you're going to change your life, it has to come from you. You have to be audacious. You have to create opportunities. You have to take action.

A rented apartment doesn't create ambition. Ambition creates ambition.

Move out when it makes sense for your finances, your growth, and your goals, not because somebody on the internet convinced you that suffering is a prerequisite for success.

content:
If you told me 10-15 years ago that I’d pay off all my student debt, retire my wife, and build the life I’m living now, I wouldn’t have believed you.

Not because I didn’t want those things badly enough, but because the version of me back then wasn’t capable of doing it.

That guy was still treating trading like a casino, taking impulsive trades, and had no real structure.

He didn’t have the discipline.

He didn’t have the experience.

He didn’t have the mindset.

And to be completely honest, he just didn’t have the knowledge or skills to achieve that type of success.

From that point of view, to think that I could become a full-time trader made no sense.

And that’s the mistake most traders make.

They limit what they can do in the future based on where they are now.

They sit where they are today and ask:

How am I going to do all of this? 

How am I going to make it work? 

How am I going to get to that level when I keep messing up?

They base their future potential on their current flaws.

But the version of you that’s crushing it in the markets is not the same version of you reading this right now, full of doubt, frustration, impatience, and habits that still need to be broken. 

That version of you is a completely different person.

And as hard as it is to believe right now, from them, making money in the markets is pretty easy.

That future version of you won’t appear overnight. 

They’re created little by little through the process.

So stop obsessing over how you’re going to pull off the end result from where you are right now.

That is not your job.

Your only job is to become the person who can.

Because once you become that person, the results that feel impossible to you today start feeling like the easiest thing in the world.

i just got off a call with the man behind all of @moonpay's social media accounts.

he's pulling in north of 100m views every month across X, Instagram, Linkedin, and Tiktok.

i genuinely consider him to be one of the legends in this space, and i wanted to share 6 of the biggest lessons he gave me about growing an audience on X.

unlike the other big brand in the crypto scene (won't name but yk who I'm talking abt)

moonpay has managed to become one of the most recognizable and more importantly one of the most liked brands in crypto.

let's get into it:

1. post more, think less

this is obviously a given and one of my favorite sayings. context on x has a short life span, people see your post and forget about it the next day, the key is to post a lot and the good posts naturally  rise to the top.

2. more storytelling, less product

i'm in charge of growing the flex X account, so this was actually super valuable to me.

i've mostly been posting only product content, but he suggested talking more about the story behind flex and leaning into invoking emotions and feelings rather than just features.

for us, that means speaking more about our tagline, "flex fuels ambition" and sharing more of that path to success that flex enables.

3. there is no perfect time to post

i already knew this, but hearing it from the man behind moonpay reinforced it.

the myth that there's a magical posting time is bullshit.

i've had posts go viral at 2am and i've had posts go viral in the middle of the afternoon.

for X at least, timing matters far less than most people think.

4. engage with every single person

sounds obvious but this tip has a lot of psychology rooted into it.

people are on social media because they want to be validated and seen. they want attention.

when a big brand account with a gold checkmark likes a post or replies to a comment, it builds a surprising amount of what I like to call "relationship equity".

over time these interactions compound into immense brand affinity.

my own little tip of advice to throw in here is to always respond with a question to prolong the talk.

when someone responds and the conversation continues x sees genuine back and forth engagement rather than a one off interaction.

the X algo eats this shit up like crazy and increases reach.

5. you don't need a big team

i assumed moonpay had a social team of 5-10 people.

wrong.

it's essentially Sean himself and one other girl helping manage everything.

they produce dozens of pieces of content everyday on top of interacting with thousands of people across 4 different social channels.

I struggle keeping up with just mine and the flex account  and was thinking of getting an assistant, hearing that Sean does this all basically by himself was insane to me.

6. be chronically online

his final piece of advice was simple, be chronically online. active at all times during the day.

could be posting, replying, commenting, dming, literally anything.

growing a  brand really comes down to just an insane volume output of good quality content.

key word good. not excellent. 

the more people you engage with, the more people know you which means the more people like you.

getting 30 minutes of his time to learn how he thinks about growing brands at scale was incredibly valuable.

I also want to point out I offered to pay Sean a consultation fee for his time and he declined, instead opting in to helping me out for free.
